name: Anabolic diet / high calorie eating

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic plan described in a 1995 book by powerlifter and writer Mauro Di Pasquale, nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet. People use it, along with other heavy-eating approaches, to eat enough to support training and gain muscle size.

It works by alternating low-carbohydrate stretches with higher-carbohydrate periods while keeping calories high, so training is fueled and mass can be added. No studies of its effect on appearance were found, and sources specific to it are limited.

paras: People follow it as a repeating weekly pattern of low-carb eating followed by higher-carb eating, alongside heavy lifting. It is usually run as a bulking phase, and size changes show up over weeks to months of consistent training and eating.

No clinical studies of the diet were found, and the sources reviewed document no risks specific to it. Like other very low-carb and very high-calorie plans, it can be hard to sustain and may not suit people with medical conditions or those on medication; a clinician can advise.

angle.text: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic low-carb, high-calorie bodybuilding plan used to fuel hard training and push muscle gain. The route to a bigger look runs through eating enough to support training and add mass. No studies of its appearance results were found.

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet (CKD) described in Mauro Di Pasquale's 1995 book of the same name and nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet. Lifters use it to add muscle while staying lean, so that the physique looks fuller and harder without excess fat. The wider practice of eating in a calorie surplus to gain size is known in bodybuilding as bulking.

Its structure, as summarised by Healthline, alternates low-carbohydrate weekdays, with roughly 60 to 65 percent of calories from fat, with high-carbohydrate weekends of roughly 60 to 80 percent carbohydrate.[1] Di Pasquale named it for the idea that carbohydrate cycling could mimic some effects of anabolic steroids, and argues that saturated fat supports hormone production.[1]

No published trial has tested the Anabolic Diet for appearance or muscle outcomes, and Healthline's review cites only animal studies on low-carbohydrate, high-fat eating.[1] Di Pasquale, born in 1945, is an Italian-born Canadian powerlifter who won the IPF World Powerlifting Championships in 1976 and the World Games in 1981.
infobox: Very low carbohydrate, high fat, high protein[1]

paras: Di Pasquale advocates low-carbohydrate diets and wrote for the bodybuilding press; his books include Drug Use and Detection in Amateur Sports (1984), The Anabolic Diet (1995), Amino Acids and Proteins for the Athlete (1997) and The Metabolic Diet (2000). He worked on writing, research and product development for the supplement company EAS from 1997 to 1999 and later worked as a drug-testing official in professional wrestling.

As described by Healthline, the plan has a maintenance or induction stage of about four weeks at roughly 18 calories per pound of body weight, a bulking stage that continues toward a target weight, and a cutting stage that lowers intake by 500 to 1,000 calories from maintenance until body fat falls below about 10 percent.[1] On weekdays carbohydrate is capped at about 30 g a day, with fat around 60 to 65 percent and protein 30 to 35 percent of calories; on weekends carbohydrate rises to roughly 60 to 80 percent.[1]
Proponents say the cycling makes the body burn more fat for fuel while sparing muscle and that calories need not be restricted.[1]

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article describes bulking as eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle, with the size of the surplus set by goals. Clean bulking aims to add muscle with little fat and often alternates higher and lower calorie days, while dirty bulking involves a large surplus with little tracking and typically adds significant fat, requiring a harder cut afterward. Protein intakes of 25 to 30 percent of calories are suggested but debated, and some bodybuilders eat five to seven meals a day to manage large food volumes.

Cyclic ketogenic dieting alternates stretches of very low carbohydrate intake with higher-carbohydrate periods. Low-carbohydrate eating is defined by thresholds that vary by organisation, such as under 20 percent of calories for the American Academy of Family Physicians, and the ketogenic diet was first used for drug-resistant childhood epilepsy in the 1920s.

Wikipedia reports that short- and medium-term weight loss on these diets can exceed that on low-fat diets by a small margin that diminishes over time, and that a 2022 Cochrane review found no advantage over balanced diets at two years. It also says low-carbohydrate diets can reduce endurance capacity for intense exercise and that depleted muscle glycogen replenishes only slowly on them.
No studies found testing the Anabolic Diet for appearance or muscle outcomes.

A 1992 randomized trial gave 40 hyperlipidemic patients a diet it labelled anabolic, with 45 to 47 percent of energy from fat and 560 to 620 mg of cholesterol, for six weeks, randomly adding either pyruvate (n=19) or a polyglucose placebo (n=21). Plasma cholesterol and LDL cholesterol fell by 4 and 5 percent in the pyruvate group but were unchanged on placebo, and resting heart rate, diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product fell 9, 6 and 12 percent with pyruvate. The trial measured blood lipids and heart-rate parameters rather than muscle, and its diet is described by that name in the paper rather than being identified there as Di Pasquale's. [2]

Wikipedia lists constipation, headache, bad breath, muscle cramps and weakness as reported effects of very low-carbohydrate diets, with long-term use linked to increases in total and LDL cholesterol; the American College of Cardiology advises discussing very low-carbohydrate diets with a clinician. Healthline notes the Anabolic Diet is low in fibre, fruit and legumes and high in saturated fat, and says it is not recommended for competitive athletes with higher carbohydrate needs or for weight loss alone.[1]

A content analysis of the 2009 issues of Men's Health found frequent advice to raise calorie intake (183 references) and protein intake (262 references) to augment muscle mass, described by the authors as an anabolic diet and framed within a mesomorphic body ideal.[3] On T Nation, members describe high-protein, high-fat eating and jokingly call steak and eggs the most anabolic diet.[4][5]

lore.intro: On T Nation, the word anabolic is used loosely for high-protein, higher-fat or surplus eating rather than strictly for Di Pasquale's cycled plan.[4][5]
